A.explanation: Moving the screen further away increases the spacing of the seven spots on the screen but does not change the diffraction angles, so no new orders are formed.

B.explanation: Higher frequency means shorter wavelength $\lambda$, so $n_{max} = d/\lambda$ increases and more orders satisfy $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$.

C.explanation: Higher intensity makes the existing seven bright spots brighter but does not change $d$, $\lambda$ or the allowed values of $n$.

D.explanation: More lines per metre means smaller slit separation $d$, so $n_{max} = d/\lambda$ decreases and fewer bright spots can be seen.

hints: Notice seven spots means zero order plus three orders each side, so the largest visible order is $n = 3$ limited by $\sin\theta \le 1$.
Recall the grating equation $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ and that the maximum possible order is $n_{max} = d/\lambda$ when $\sin\theta = 1$.
Compare how each change affects $d$ or $\lambda$: ask whether $d/\lambda$ gets larger, which would allow $n = 4$ or higher to exist.
walkthrough: Seven bright spots are $n = 0$ in the centre plus $n = 1, 2, 3$ on each side, so currently $n = 3$ is just visible but $n = 4$ gives $\sin\theta > 1$.
Use the grating rule $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, where $d$ is slit separation and $\lambda$ is wavelength of the single-frequency light.
The limiting case is $\sin\theta = 1$ at 90 degrees, giving maximum order $n_{max} = d/\lambda$; only integer $n \le n_{max}$ appear.
Increasing frequency $f$ decreases wavelength because $\lambda = c/f$, so denominator $\lambda$ gets smaller and $n_{max} = d/\lambda$ gets larger.
A larger $n_{max}$ can allow the next integer order beyond $n = 3$ to satisfy $\sin\theta \le 1$, adding a new pair of spots.
Increasing screen distance only magnifies positions, increasing intensity only brightens spots, and increasing lines per metre decreases $d$ which decreases $n_{max}$.
Only increased frequency increases $d/\lambda$ and the count of visible orders. This is option B.
